description: We're HARK, space enthusiasts tackling the Space Mission Game challenge. We love mission design, strategy, and turning real aerospace concepts into playable experiences. Our skills include mission planning, systems thinking, game design, prototyping, and space research. Join us if you enjoy strategy, simulation, and solving problems under constraints we build fast and make space decisions fun. We're looking for game developers, UI/UX designers, space science enthusiasts, narrative designers.
summary: Galaxy Run is a free browser game that teaches space mission design by explaining why a mission worked or failed. Players pick a scenario (Earth, the Moon or Mars), build a spacecraft from a bus, instruments, launcher, antenna and orbit, and watch live bars for mass, power, cost and data. After launch, seeded random events such as solar flares and communication dropouts test the design. A mission report then ties every result to a decision, with a cause, an effect and a fix. The game answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by letting learners try, fail, change the design and try again. It helps students and teachers understand the trade-offs between mass, power, budget, data and risk, with one public link and no install.
details:
What it does: One player designs and flies a full space mission. They choose a scenario, build the spacecraft and review the design. Live bars show mass, power, cost, data and schedule, and launch stays locked until the design passes review. The mission then runs on a timeline with seeded random events, so the same design and seed always give the same result. A report scores science return, efficiency, reliability and a learning bonus.
Benefits and impact: Most tools teach one concept at a time, and most games only say "you failed". Galaxy Run connects the concepts, because mass, power and money compete for the same limits. Every warning and report card gives a cause, an effect and a fix in plain words. A mission takes about ten minutes, so it fits one class.
Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Vitest and Vercel. The simulation engine is plain TypeScript with no interface code, so every rule is testable.
Creativity: The "why engine". Every rule returns a number and a reason, and the interface only shows reasons the engine produced, so explanations always match the numbers.
Team considerations: accuracy (real formulas with simplifications stated), fairness (seeded events), ease of learning (Easy mode, guided first mission, tooltips) and access (one link, laptop and tablet).
